input.cautions:
Where the literature disagrees, and where it fits this system badly.

1. Deming is routinely over-read. Point 3 says cease dependence on inspection *on a mass basis* and eliminate the *need* for it by building quality in — it is not an argument against all checking. Deming himself supplied the kp rule, which prescribes 100% inspection when the defect rate exceeds k1/k2, and he defended checking at the point of production. So "the corpus has too many checks" cannot be settled by quoting Deming; it must be settled by measuring pass rates and costs. A check that never fails anything is the target; a check that catches real defects cheaply is not. This cuts against a sweeping reading of H2.

2. Documentation is not the enemy, and DORA is the best evidence for that. DORA's documentation-quality findings are among the strongest effect sizes in the whole corpus of delivery research — teams with good internal documentation get multiples more value from every technical practice. So a finding of "too much documentation" must be stated as a findability/reliability/clarity failure or as a debt ratio, not as volume. Beware the reviewer's trap of treating word count as the pathology: RegData's contribution was showing that restriction counts track burden where page counts do not. This complicates H1: the problem is very likely obligation count and unreproducible judgment, not verbosity per se.

3. Formal quality systems have genuinely mixed empirical support. ISO 9001 studies split: meta-analyses find revenue and process benefits in many cases, no reliable cost benefit, and several large samples find no significant performance difference at all. Any claim that "governance systems like this don't work" overstates the evidence; the honest statement is that formal systems help when coupled to the work and do nothing (or harm) when decoupled from it — which is precisely Meyer & Rowan's point and why decoupling, not documentation, is the variable to measure.

4. Flow efficiency benchmarks are soft. The 5–15% typical / 15–25% good figures circulate widely but rest on practitioner surveys and consultancy data, not controlled studies; the underlying definition of "value-added time" is contested, and Nick Brown's own ASOS write-ups argue the metric is frequently gamed and misapplied. Use flow efficiency as a within-system trend and a conversation-opener, not as a pass/fail gate against an external number.

5. DORA's four keys do not transfer cleanly to a definition corpus. They were derived and validated for teams deploying software to production; a shop producing governance artifacts has no deployments, so any "DORA score" here is an analogy, not a measurement. What does transfer is the structural claim — throughput and stability move together in healthy systems — and the 2024 finding that this co-movement can break, which should caution against treating any single derived metric as diagnostic. The 2025 DORA "AI amplifies existing conditions" finding is survey-based and correlational; it is a useful frame, not proof.

6. Measuring this system risks the very dysfunction the sources warn about. Ridgway (1956), Campbell, and Strathern's Goodhart formulation all predict that publishing these factors as targets inside a system already inclined to generate conformance evidence will produce artifacts optimised against the factors. Mitigations: keep the factor set plural (SPACE's rule: at least three dimensions, never one number), keep at least one factor externally observed rather than self-reported, and re-derive the numbers independently rather than accepting the system's own tally. If these factors become an eighth check inside the corpus, they have failed.

7. The bureaucracy literature is largely about large organisations and has a strong prior against process. March/Schulz/Zhou studied a university over decades; Bozeman studied public agencies; Hamel & Zanini's BMI is a self-selected HBR-reader survey (n≈7,000, not a random sample) with an explicit anti-bureaucracy thesis. Applied to a 26-day-old, one-human, agent-staffed shop, these give mechanisms and vocabulary, not calibrated thresholds. Every numeric threshold in the factors above is either taken from a different domain (SQALE's 5%, DORA's bands) or proposed by me as a starting line; treat them as prompts for judgment, not as grades.

8. Two structural features of this system have no real literature behind them and should be flagged as genuinely uncharted. First, the constraint is not labour but one human's *attention*, and the producing capacity is effectively free and unbounded — no flow model in the sources was built for a system where supply of work-product is near-infinite and review capacity is fixed at one person. Second, the LLM instruction-following benchmarks (IFScale, ComplexBench, FollowBench) measure compliance with *synthetic, independently checkable* constraints; extrapolating from keyword-inclusion tasks to "can an agent apply a judgment-laden governance principle" is a real leap. The direction of the finding (more obligations, worse adherence, earlier obligations favoured) is robust; the specific numbers are not transferable.

9. On the 26-day question, the literature gives two defensible and opposed readings, and a reviewer should say so. The delivery frameworks (Agile, Shape Up, DORA) judge 26 days with no output harshly and unambiguously. The institutional and standards literature would say a foundation-laying phase producing no external output is normal and that judging it by delivery metrics is a category error. The tiebreaker available here is not a rule but an evidentiary one: was the foundation *tested* against anything external in that period? A foundation validated only by its own checks has no claim on the second reading — which is where the strongest finding in this analysis sits, and it does not depend on any particular threshold being right.

factors.name: Time to first working output
factors.question: How long since the system started, and has it produced one thing a user of the product could run or use?
factors.source: Agile Manifesto, Principles behind the Manifesto (2001), principles 1, 3, 7: "deliver working software frequently, from a couple of weeks to a couple of months, with a preference to the shorter timescale" and "Working software is the primary measure of progress" — https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html. Ryan Singer, Shape Up (Basecamp, 2019), ch. 6 "Set boundaries" (appetite) — https://basecamp.com/shapeup/1.5-chapter-06.
factors.measurement: Elapsed calendar days since the effort started, divided by the declared appetite. Count as output only artifacts consumed outside the system that produces them. Score: <1.0 appetite = on track; 1.0–2.0 = overrun, circuit-breaker decision due; >2.0 with zero output = failed. Observed here: 26 days, 280 commits, 471k words of corpus, 4,461 lines of Python — all of it tooling that compiles and lints the corpus itself; zero product-facing software. No declared appetite found for the rebaseline as a whole, which is itself a finding (a system with no appetite cannot trip a circuit breaker).
factors.why: Every delivery framework in the literature uses shipped output, not produced documents, as the progress signal. A system that produces only its own definitions has no external observation correcting it; the only feedback is internal review, which is the condition Meyer & Rowan describe as ceremonial. 26 days with no output is below the DORA low-performer band (deploy once per month to once per six months), i.e. it does not yet appear on the delivery-performance scale at all.

factors.name: Circuit breaker: declared appetite and enforced expiry
factors.question: Is there a fixed time box on the current effort, and what actually happens when it is exceeded — cancellation and reshaping, or extension by default?
factors.source: Ryan Singer, Shape Up, ch. 8 "The betting table", section "The circuit breaker": "Teams have to ship the work within the amount of time that we bet. If they don't finish, by default the project doesn't get an extension" and "only betting one cycle at a time and never carrying scraps of old work over without first shaping and considering them as a new potential bet" — https://basecamp.com/shapeup/2.2-chapter-08. Also ch. 6 on fixed time / variable scope.
factors.measurement: Count: (a) efforts currently in flight with a written appetite; (b) efforts that have passed their appetite; (c) of those, how many were cancelled vs extended. Healthy per Shape Up: extension is the exception and requires a fresh bet; cancellation is the default. Red flag: extension rate ≥ 50%, or appetite absent, or scope fixed while time floats — the exact inversion Shape Up names.
factors.why: The appetite is the only mechanism in Shape Up that forces scope reduction; a system that claims Shape Up but never cancels has imported the vocabulary without the constraint. This is the cleanest test of whether a stated model is operative or ceremonial, and it discriminates directly: a real circuit breaker leaves a record of things killed. If no artifact in 26 days was killed for exceeding its appetite, the model is not in force.

factors.name: Flow efficiency (value-added share of elapsed time)
factors.question: Of the elapsed time from a request entering the system to something leaving it, what fraction was spent adding value the consumer would pay for?
factors.source: Flow efficiency / process cycle efficiency, Lean: value-added time ÷ total lead time. Benchmarks: most knowledge-work teams 5–15%; 15–25% considered good; >40% rare — Kanban University, "Flow Efficiency: A great metric you probably aren't using" (https://resources.kanban.university/flow-efficiency-a-great-metric-you-probably-arent-using/); Nick Brown, "Our survey says… uncovering the real numbers behind flow efficiency", ASOS Tech Blog (https://medium.com/asos-techblog/our-survey-says-uncovering-the-real-numbers-behind-flow-efficiency-e54f136b1fab). Donald Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) on invisible queues as the largest source of waste.
factors.measurement: Pick 5 completed items end to end. For each, timestamp entry and exit and mark each interval as touch time or wait time (waiting on approval, on a clarification round, on a check, on a rendering/compile step). Flow efficiency = touch ÷ elapsed. Also compute a governance-specific variant: fraction of touch time spent on the item itself vs on satisfying the process about the item. Red flag: the second number exceeding the first.
factors.why: Flow efficiency separates 'people are busy' from 'work is moving'. It is the metric that exposes a bottleneck without needing anyone to admit to one, and it is the direct quantitative test of H5. Crucially it is measurable from existing records (commit and session timestamps) without new instrumentation.

factors.name: Bottleneck concentration on the single human
factors.question: What share of work items must pass through the one human decision-maker, and what is the queue in front of that person?
factors.source: Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal (1984) and the Five Focusing Steps: identify, exploit, subordinate, elevate, repeat — Theory of Constraints Institute (https://www.tocinstitute.org/five-focusing-steps.html); Lean Enterprise Institute overview (https://www.lean.org/the-lean-post/articles/what-is-the-theory-of-constraints-and-how-does-it-compare-to-lean-thinking/). Little's Law for queue length ↔ wait time.
factors.measurement: Count defined process steps that require the authority's decision, as a fraction of all steps; count items waiting on that person at a given moment; measure mean wait per approval. TOC test of whether the constraint is being exploited: what fraction of the authority's attention goes to irreversible, high-value decisions (bets, direction) vs to reviewing conformance of documents to rules (work a subordinate step should have absorbed)? Red flag: >30% of the constraint's time on conformance review; approval queue longer than 1 cycle of work.
factors.why: TOC's 'subordinate' step says non-constraints must not run faster than the constraint. A generative agent fleet is an effectively unbounded non-constraint: it can produce definitions faster than one human can read them. Unless subordination is explicit, the system will convert the fleet's capacity into queue in front of the human — which looks like productivity and is pure inventory. This factor distinguishes 'the human is busy' (fine) from 'the human is the only place decisions can be made and the queue is growing' (fatal).

factors.name: Meta-work ratio (system tending itself vs producing value)
factors.question: What proportion of total effort goes into the governance system versus into the thing the governance system exists to produce?
factors.source: Gary Hamel & Michele Zanini, "What We Learned About Bureaucracy from 7,000 HBR Readers", HBR, August 2017 — the Bureaucracy Mass Index and its seven cost categories: bloat, friction, insularity, disempowerment, risk aversion, inertia, politics (https://hbr.org/2017/08/what-we-learned-about-bureaucracy-from-7000-hbr-readers). 'Insularity' = time spent on internal rather than external issues.
factors.measurement: Partition every commit, word, and hour into: (A) product-facing output, (B) definitions/process/tooling about how the work is done, (C) records about work done. Compute B+C ÷ total. Observed here: basis/ 140k words + requests/decisions/briefs/sessions 130k words, product-facing software 0; 100% of the 4,461 lines of Python are corpus compilers, linters and cost-rollups. A ratio above ~0.5 sustained past the first cycle is Hamel & Zanini's insularity in numeric form; here it is ≈1.0.
factors.why: This is the single most discriminating number available without new instrumentation, and it is hard to argue with. A healthy shop's governance is a minority of its mass; a pathological one's governance is the product. It also usefully refutes a naive reading of 'no output': this system has produced a great deal of software, all of it aimed at itself.

factors.name: Rule accretion vs rule retirement
factors.question: Over the period, how many rules were added, how many were changed, and how many were deleted or suspended?
factors.source: James G. March, Martin Schulz & Xueguang Zhou, The Dynamics of Rules: Change in Written Organizational Codes (Stanford University Press, 2000) — birth, change and suspension of written rules in the Stanford archive; rule births respond to attention and to problems, and rule suspension is rare relative to rule birth (https://www.sup.org/books/title/?id=388). Barry Bozeman, Bureaucracy and Red Tape (2000) on rule-evolved red tape.
factors.measurement: From version control: count rules/obligations added, amended, and removed per week. Compute the retirement ratio = removals ÷ additions. Healthy: non-trivial and roughly stable over time. Red flag: retirement ratio ≈ 0 over a full cycle, i.e. the corpus is monotonic. Also compute rule half-life: median age at which a rule is revisited at all. Observed here: 129 MUST, 28 MUST NOT obligations in force; git history shows repeated additive approval batches; no recorded retirement event was found in the corpus's own terms (retirement exists only as a planned migration action).
factors.why: March et al.'s core empirical result is that written codes grow because birth is easy and death is hard — no one is accountable for a rule that is merely unnecessary. A monotonic rule count is therefore the expected null trajectory for any rule-making system, not evidence of anything going wrong, which is why you must measure the retirement ratio explicitly: it is the only observable that separates a system that is learning from one that is silting up.

factors.name: Red-tape share of standing rules
factors.question: Which standing rules impose compliance burden without serving the purpose they were written to serve?
factors.source: Barry Bozeman's definition: red tape is "rules, regulations, and procedures that remain in force and entail a compliance burden but [do] not advance the legitimate purposes the rules were intended to serve"; the distinction between rule-inception red tape (born bad) and rule-evolved red tape (once useful, now not) — Bozeman, Bureaucracy and Red Tape (Prentice Hall, 2000); overview: GWU Regulatory Studies Center, "Red Tape Literature in Public Administration" (2022), https://regulatorystudies.columbian.gwu.edu/red-tape-literature-public-administration. Meta-analysis of effects: Blom, Borst & Voorn, "Pathology or Inconvenience?", Review of Public Personnel Administration 41(4), 2021.
factors.measurement: Sample 10 obligations at random. For each ask: name one concrete failure this rule prevented in the last 30 days, with the record that shows it. Score as served / unserved / unknown. Red-tape share = (unserved + unknown) ÷ 10. Threshold: >50% unserved-or-unknown means the majority of the rule mass is unaudited cost.
factors.why: It converts 'too much process' from an aesthetic complaint into an evidentiary one, and it is symmetrical — a rule that has caught real defects survives the test. It also directly probes H4 from the other side: a rule that is routinely waived and whose waiver produced no harm is by Bozeman's definition red tape, and the right response is deletion, not tighter enforcement.

factors.name: Normative density (restriction count per 1,000 words; MUST:SHOULD ratio)
factors.question: How many binding obligations does the corpus contain per unit of text, and what fraction of its normative language is absolute rather than discretionary?
factors.source: RFC 2119 / BCP 14, §6 Guidance in the use of these Imperatives: "Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm … they must not be used to try to impose a particular method on implementors where the method is not required for interoperability" — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119.txt. Counting restrictions as a measure of regulatory burden: Al-Ubaydli & McLaughlin, "RegData: A numerical database on industry-specific regulations for all United States industries and federal regulations, 1997–2012", Regulation & Governance 11(1), 2017 — counts of shall, must, may not, required, prohibited (https://www.mercatus.org/research/working-papers/regdata).
factors.measurement: grep -c the RFC 2119 keyword set; normalise per 1,000 words; compute absolute share = (MUST + MUST NOT + SHALL) ÷ all keywords. Observed here: 129 MUST, 28 MUST NOT, 5 SHOULD, 13 MAY → absolute share 90%, discretionary share 3%. Then apply the RFC 2119 §6 test to a sample of MUSTs: does this obligation exist for interoperation between roles, or to prevent harm? If neither, it is method imposition, which BCP 14 explicitly rules out. Red flag: absolute share >80%, or >20% of sampled MUSTs failing the §6 test.
factors.why: Directly tests H6, and does so using the adopted convention's own terms rather than an outside standard. RegData's contribution is showing that restriction counts track real burden better than page counts do — so this is a better length proxy than word count, and it explains why a corpus can be both 'not that long' and crushing. A 26:1 MUST:SHOULD ratio in documents whose stated purpose is improving judgment is a self-contradiction on the face of the text.

factors.name: Obligation load in the generating context
factors.question: How many independently checkable obligations are loaded into a single agent's context at once, and does compliance degrade at that count?
factors.source: Jaroslawicz et al., "How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once?" (IFScale benchmark), arXiv:2507.11538 — 20 frontier models, 500 keyword-inclusion instructions; best models reach only 68% accuracy at 500 instructions, with a measurable primacy bias toward earlier instructions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11538). Wen et al., "Benchmarking Complex Instruction-Following with Multiple Constraints Composition" (ComplexBench), NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2407.03978. Jiang et al., FollowBench — accuracy measured level by level as one constraint is added at a time.
factors.measurement: Count the distinct obligations in the compiled session block plus the loaded skill/process prompt for one representative activity (count each MUST-bullet as one). Then run the empirical test the benchmarks model: take 10 recent outputs produced under that context and score each against every obligation; compliance rate = satisfied ÷ (obligations × outputs). Compare with the same agent given only the 5 most load-bearing obligations. Red flag: compliance below ~85%, or no measurable improvement in output quality from the extra obligations — the latter means the additional rules are cost with no yield.
factors.why: This is the version of H1 that can be settled with evidence rather than taste. The benchmark literature establishes that obligation count, not document length, is what degrades adherence, and that degradation is graded rather than cliff-edged — so a corpus can be simultaneously 'all reasonable rules' and unfollowable. Primacy bias also predicts a specific pathology worth checking for: late-loaded rules (typically the domain-specific ones) are the ones silently dropped.

factors.name: Independence of the check
factors.question: For each check in the system, is the checker structurally independent of the party whose work is being checked?
factors.source: IIA, The Three Lines Model: An Update of the Three Lines of Defense (July 2020) — independence of the third line requires that assurance providers have no current or recent responsibility for the activity assessed (https://www.theiia.org/globalassets/documents/resources/the-iias-three-lines-model-an-update-of-the-three-lines-of-defense-july-2020/three-lines-model-updated-english.pdf). ISO 19011 impartiality principle; ISO 9001 clause 9.2 (auditors shall not audit their own work).
factors.measurement: Enumerate every check step. Classify the checker as: (1) same agent/role as maker, (2) different role but same context/prompt lineage, (3) fresh context, different accountability, (4) external party. Independence score = share in classes 3–4. Then count approval stamps by class. Red flag: any state transition that the maker can set on its own work (observed here: 'self-check' appears 325 times across the corpus; a feature is set `checked` by the PO that authored it, and fitness screens are asserted in-document by the author).
factors.why: The assurance literature is unambiguous that self-assessment is not assurance; it is documentation of intent. This factor tests H4 at its structural root and explains why the corpus's own principle ("the check MUST sit with a different role holding a different accountability") can be textually satisfied while functionally void — different role, same generating context, same interest in passing.

factors.name: Reproducibility of a passing verdict
factors.question: If the same artifact is re-checked in a fresh context by a different evaluator, does it get the same verdict?
factors.source: Michael Power, The Audit Society: Rituals of Verification (Oxford University Press, 1997) — audit generates comfort rather than knowledge; organisations reshape themselves to be auditable; audit processes can become "a world in itself, self-referentially creating auditable images of performance" (https://academic.oup.com/book/26482). V. F. Ridgway, "Dysfunctional Consequences of Performance Measurements", Administrative Science Quarterly 1(2), 1956, 240–247 (summary: https://maaw.info/ArticleSummaries/ArtSumRidgway56.htm).
factors.measurement: Take 5 artifacts recorded as passing. Re-run the stated check in a fresh context with no access to the original verdict. Agreement rate = identical verdicts ÷ 5. Healthy: ≥80% with disagreements traceable to a named ambiguity. Red flag: <60%, or the check cannot be re-run at all because the evidence of the original pass is a prose assertion rather than a reproducible procedure.
factors.why: This is the operational definition of the difference between governance that produces quality and governance that produces artifacts about quality. A verdict nobody can reproduce carries no information; it only carries comfort, which is exactly Power's finding. It is also the cheapest high-yield experiment available to the reviewer — five re-runs settle an argument that could otherwise run for weeks.

factors.name: Inspection position and economic justification
factors.question: Is quality being built in at the point of making, or inspected in afterwards — and does the defect rate justify the inspection cost?
factors.source: W. Edwards Deming, Out of the Crisis (MIT CAES, 1986), Point 3: "Cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality. Eliminate the need for inspection on a mass basis by building quality into the product in the first place" (https://deming.org/explore/fourteen-points/); "Inspection is too late. The quality, good or bad, is already in the product" (https://deming.org/inspection-is-too-late-the-quality-good-or-bad-is-already-in-the-product/). Deming's kp rule: with k1 = cost to inspect one unit and k2 = cost of a defect escaping, inspect none if the defect fraction p < k1/k2, inspect 100% if p > k1/k2 (Deming Inspection Criterion; see Journal of Quality Technology 17(3), 1985).
factors.measurement: For each standing check: record (a) items checked in the last 30 days, (b) items failed, (c) hours spent checking, (d) estimated cost of an escape. p = b ÷ a. Break-even = (hours per check × rate) ÷ escape cost. Red flag: p ≈ 0 with substantial checking cost — the check is uneconomic by Deming's own criterion and should be replaced by better inputs (better guidelines, better exemplars, better tooling at the point of making). Equally red: a check that never fails anything is not a check, it is a ceremony.
factors.why: It sharpens H2 without needing to settle the author's intent. Even granting that checks are wanted, Deming gives a quantitative test for whether a given check pays, and most corpus checks in a system like this will fail it — their pass rate is ~100% because the maker and the checker share a generating context. The remedy Deming prescribes (improve the process that makes the thing) is also the remedy that reduces corpus mass, so the factor points at a fix rather than only a fault.

factors.name: Ceremonial conformity / decoupling
factors.question: How many defined processes have actually been executed end to end, and how far do the records diverge from what was really done?
factors.source: John W. Meyer & Brian Rowan, "Institutionalized Organizations: Formal Structure as Myth and Ceremony", American Journal of Sociology 83(2), 1977, 340–363 — institutionalised practices are adopted ceremonially for legitimacy, and formal structure is decoupled from actual activity, sustained by a "logic of confidence" (http://www.iot.ntnu.no/innovation/norsi-pims-courses/harrison/Meyer%20&%20Rowan%20(1977).PDF). Power (1997) on decoupling in audit.
factors.measurement: For each defined process: number of complete executions; date of last execution; number of steps skipped in the most recent execution; whether the record says the step ran. Compute never-run share = processes with zero end-to-end executions ÷ all processes. Observed here: 25 process definitions totalling 63,009 words; several (implementation, scenario-assignment, reconcile-and-close, bc-emit paths) are unexecutable by construction because the shop is frozen. Red flag: never-run share >40%, or any case where the record asserts a step ran that left no artifact.
factors.why: Defining processes that cannot run is the purest form of the pathology: the definition earns legitimacy now and is never disciplined by contact with execution. Meyer & Rowan predict exactly this when the environment rewards having the right structures rather than the right outcomes — and a self-defining shop is an environment in which the only audience for the structure is the structure.

factors.name: Quality-attribute coverage of the built artifact
factors.question: Does the corpus say anything about what a good built thing looks like, or only about what a good process looks like?
factors.source: ISO/IEC 25010:2023, Systems and software engineering — SQuaRE — Product quality model: nine characteristics — functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability, reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility, safety (https://www.iso.org/standard/78176.html; change summary: https://quality.arc42.org/articles/iso-25010-update-2023).
factors.measurement: Map every principle and guideline onto the nine ISO 25010 characteristics; count how many are addressed with stated criteria. Then classify each principle as process-governing (about how work proceeds) or artifact-governing (about the properties of the thing produced). Red flag: artifact-governing share near zero. Observed here: the six implementation principles (`built-to-the-scenario`, `effect-shown`, `effect-not-mechanism`, `nothing-lost`, `knowable-from-the-record`, `cost-on-the-initiative`) are all process-governing; across the whole basis/ tree there are zero occurrences of maintainability, modularity, cohesion, reliability, performance efficiency or security as quality criteria, and one occurrence of 'coupling'. H3 is confirmed on the evidence.
factors.why: This is the decisive test of whether a governance system can produce quality at all. If no rule constrains the properties of the product, then every rule constrains only the paperwork around it, and passing the whole system is compatible with building something bad. ISO 25010 gives a neutral, external checklist so the finding is not a matter of opinion, and the 2023 revision is the current form, which matters for a corpus that claims external-standards-first.

factors.name: Documentation quality: clarity, findability, reliability
factors.question: Can the person or agent who needs a definition find it, understand it, and trust it to be current?
factors.source: DORA, Capabilities: Documentation quality — quality measured on three attributes (clarity, findability, reliability) via eight survey items; quality documentation amplifies the organisational-performance effect of technical capabilities (reported amplifications include continuous integration and trunk-based development by large multiples) (https://dora.dev/capabilities/documentation-quality/). 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps Report (https://dora.dev/research/2024/dora-report/).
factors.measurement: Task test, not opinion: give a fresh agent 5 real tasks; for each, record time-to-locate the governing definition, number of documents opened, and whether the answer found was current. Also compute a staleness measure: share of documents whose stated source-digest or referenced definition no longer matches. Healthy: right document found first or second try, <5 minutes, current. Red flag: multiple documents must be reconciled to answer one question — that is a findability failure even when every document is individually correct.
factors.why: DORA is the strongest empirical evidence that documentation quality is a force multiplier rather than overhead — which is a genuine counterweight to 'this corpus is too big'. But DORA measures documentation by whether users can use it, not by whether it is complete or governed. A corpus that scores badly on findability while scoring perfectly on internal consistency has optimised the wrong variable, and this factor says so with the authority of the pro-documentation literature rather than against it.

factors.name: Governance debt ratio
factors.question: What would it cost to bring the governance corpus to a state its own users could work from, relative to what it cost to build?
factors.source: SQALE / SonarQube technical debt ratio: remediation cost ÷ development cost, with maintainability rating A at ≤5%, B ≤10%, C ≤20%, D ≤50% (https://docs.sonarsource.com/sonarqube-server/user-guide/code-metrics/metrics-definition). Process debt as a first-class debt type: Martini, Besker & Bosch, "Process Debt: A First Exploration", APSEC 2020; Martini, Stray, Besker, Moe & Bosch, "Process Debt: Definition, Risks and Management" (2024). Documentation debt in the TD taxonomy: Alves et al. (2016); Rios et al., tertiary study (2018).
factors.measurement: Estimate remediation effort (hours to simplify, deduplicate, delete red tape, and make checks reproducible) ÷ effort already invested. Apply the SQALE bands: ≤5% healthy, >20% is a C, >50% means rewriting is cheaper than repairing. Supporting counts: duplicate statements of the same rule; definitions with more than one authoritative home; obligations with no executable check.
factors.why: It gives the restart decision a defensible arithmetic rather than a mood. The SQALE framing is exactly the right one for 'should we restart again': when remediation exceeds roughly half of what was invested, the literature's own grading says the asset is a D/E and rebuild becomes rational. The process-debt literature matters because it establishes that debt in the way of working behaves like code debt — it compounds, it is invisible on any delivery dashboard, and it is repaid only by deliberate removal.

factors.name: Waivability asymmetry
factors.question: For each constraint, who can waive it — and is that the same party the constraint binds?
factors.source: Bozeman on rule-evolved red tape (above); IIA Three Lines Model on independence (above); Goodhart's law in Marilyn Strathern's formulation, "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure", from "'Improving ratings': audit in the British University system", European Review 5(3), 1997, 305–321 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7901608/).
factors.measurement: Build a table: constraint | binds whom | who may waive | waivers in last 30 days | waiver recorded where. Self-waivable share = constraints whose waiver authority is the constrained party ÷ all constraints. Red flag: >25% self-waivable, or waivers recorded inside the waived artifact rather than in a register anyone sweeps. Observed here: 'accepted gap' appears 13 times, mostly as author-recorded self-exemptions; artifact tooling exists but nothing prevents bypassing it.
factors.why: A constraint the constrained party can waive is not a constraint; it is a default. This factor tests H4 as a structural property rather than by counting incidents, which matters because incidents are under-recorded precisely where waiving is easy. It also predicts which rules will decay first: the ones that cost the maker the most and whose waiver costs the maker nothing.

factors.name: Measurement dysfunction and self-reported success
factors.question: Are the system's own indicators self-reported by the party being measured, and do they move independently of delivered value?
factors.source: V. F. Ridgway, "Dysfunctional Consequences of Performance Measurements", ASQ 1(2), 1956 — single, multiple and composite measures all produce dysfunction; the employment-interviewer case (more interviews, fewer placements). Goodhart / Strathern (1997) as above. Donald Campbell's law on corruption pressure in social indicators (1979). Jerry Z. Muller, The Tyranny of Metrics (Princeton UP, 2018).
factors.measurement: For each indicator the system uses (approvals granted, checks passed, principles satisfied, fitness screens cleared), record: source of the number (self-reported vs independently observed), and correlation over time with any externally observable outcome. Red flag: all indicators internal and self-reported, all trending favourably, while external output is flat at zero. That pattern is the definition of measurement dysfunction rather than evidence of health.
factors.why: It supplies the reviewer with a stopping rule against the strongest defence such a system can mount — 'every artifact passed its check'. Ridgway's point, unchanged since 1956, is that quantitative conformance signals are reliable only when generated independently of the people they judge; here they are not.

factors.name: Clarification-round cost per unit of delivered work
factors.question: How many human interventions does one unit of work consume, and is that number falling?
factors.source: Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck & Butler, "The SPACE of Developer Productivity", ACM Queue 19(1), 2021 — five dimensions (Satisfaction and well-being; Performance; Activity; Communication and collaboration; Efficiency and flow), with the guidance to use metrics from at least three dimensions and never a single metric, and to include perceptual data alongside system data (https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3454124; primer: https://getdx.com/blog/space-framework-primer/). 2025 DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development on workflow clarity as an amplifier (https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report).
factors.measurement: Per delivered artifact, count round trips to the authority, and split them into decisions (irreducible: bets, direction, priority) and clarifications (reducible: what does this rule mean, does this satisfy that). Clarification share and its trend over successive artifacts. Healthy: clarification share falling as the corpus matures. Red flag: flat or rising — each new definition buys new ambiguity at least as fast as it resolves old ambiguity, which is H1's actual mechanism and H5's actual cause.
factors.why: It distinguishes two very different stories that look identical from the outside: a founder who is deeply engaged (healthy) and a founder who is the only resolver of ambiguity the system itself generates (fatal). The trend line is the discriminator, and it is recoverable from session records. SPACE also supplies the discipline that no one of these factors should be read alone.

factors.name: Human satisfaction and friction (the S in SPACE)
factors.question: Does the one human in the loop believe the system is helping, and is that belief trending up or down?
factors.source: SPACE framework, Satisfaction and well-being dimension (Forsgren et al., ACM Queue 2021). 2025 DORA report team profiles, including "foundational challenges" (low performance, high friction, high burnout) and "harmonious high-achievers"; and the report's central finding that AI amplifies existing team conditions rather than fixing them (https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-the-2025-dora-report; report PDF: https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/2025_state_of_ai_assisted_software_development.pdf).
factors.measurement: A short standing self-report from the authority each cycle: would you recommend this way of working; is it getting easier or harder; what fraction of your time last cycle felt like it moved the product. Track the trend, not the level. Red flag: the single stakeholder reporting the system is off course — which, in a one-human system, is not a soft signal but the primary outcome measure, because that person is simultaneously the customer, the constraint and the quality bar.
factors.why: SPACE's authors insist productivity cannot be read from activity alone in knowledge work, and the 2025 DORA data shows that high activity with high friction is a recognised, distinct and bad profile. In a system whose entire output is currently consumed by one person, their perception is not proxy evidence — it is the outcome variable, and treating it as anecdote would be a measurement error in itself.

factors.name: Batch size and feedback latency
factors.question: How large is the unit of work between one piece of external feedback and the next?
factors.source: Donald Reinertsen, The Principles of Product Development Flow (Celeritas, 2009) — batch size as an economic trade-off between transaction cost and holding cost; invisible queues as the largest source of waste; only ~2% of product developers measure queues (https://www.leanessays.com / summaries: https://joecotellese.com/posts/principles-of-product-development-flow-book-summary/). Shape Up on one-cycle bets. 2025 DORA on small batches as an AI-amplifying practice.
factors.measurement: Measure the size of approval batches (how many definitions approved in one decision), and the interval between successive contacts with reality (a run, a build, a user). Observed here: approvals arrive in batches (e.g. the product flow approved end to end "by batch under brief-032"), and the interval between corpus change and external validation is currently unbounded — no execution has occurred. Red flag: batch approvals covering more artifacts than the approver can independently verify; any feedback interval exceeding one appetite.
factors.why: Batch size governs how much can be wrong before anything is discovered. Approving a whole process chain in one batch is a large-batch decision in Reinertsen's exact sense: transaction cost falls, holding cost and error latency rise. This factor explains how 26 days of diligent work can produce a corpus that is internally coherent and externally untested — nothing in it has yet been allowed to be wrong in public.

factors.name: Definition-to-execution lag
factors.question: For each definition written, how long until something actually ran through it?
factors.source: Derived from Lean's build-quality-in argument (Deming, Point 3) combined with Shape Up's rule that shaping precedes betting by one cycle at most and unbet work is discarded rather than stockpiled (ch. 7, "Bets, not backlogs"; ch. 8). Supported by March, Schulz & Zhou on rules created from attention rather than from problems.
factors.measurement: Per definition: date approved → date first executed end to end. Compute median lag and the share still never executed. Healthy: definitions written just in time, median lag under one cycle. Red flag: median lag undefined because most definitions have never run; definitions written for activities that cannot occur under current conditions (here: the shop is frozen, yet dispatch, assignment and reconcile processes are fully specified and approved).
factors.why: Defining ahead of execution is exactly where speculative generality enters a governance corpus, and it is the mechanism that converts 'being thorough' into unrecoverable mass. This factor is more actionable than 'the corpus is too big' because it names which parts to cut first: everything with no execution and no scheduled execution.

Where the literature disagrees, and where it fits this system badly.

1. Deming is routinely over-read. Point 3 says cease dependence on inspection *on a mass basis* and eliminate the *need* for it by building quality in — it is not an argument against all checking. Deming himself supplied the kp rule, which prescribes 100% inspection when the defect rate exceeds k1/k2, and he defended checking at the point of production. So "the corpus has too many checks" cannot be settled by quoting Deming; it must be settled by measuring pass rates and costs. A check that never fails anything is the target; a check that catches real defects cheaply is not. This cuts against a sweeping reading of H2.

2. Documentation is not the enemy, and DORA is the best evidence for that. DORA's documentation-quality findings are among the strongest effect sizes in the whole corpus of delivery research — teams with good internal documentation get multiples more value from every technical practice. So a finding of "too much documentation" must be stated as a findability/reliability/clarity failure or as a debt ratio, not as volume. Beware the reviewer's trap of treating word count as the pathology: RegData's contribution was showing that restriction counts track burden where page counts do not. This complicates H1: the problem is very likely obligation count and unreproducible judgment, not verbosity per se.

3. Formal quality systems have genuinely mixed empirical support. ISO 9001 studies split: meta-analyses find revenue and process benefits in many cases, no reliable cost benefit, and several large samples find no significant performance difference at all. Any claim that "governance systems like this don't work" overstates the evidence; the honest statement is that formal systems help when coupled to the work and do nothing (or harm) when decoupled from it — which is precisely Meyer & Rowan's point and why decoupling, not documentation, is the variable to measure.

4. Flow efficiency benchmarks are soft. The 5–15% typical / 15–25% good figures circulate widely but rest on practitioner surveys and consultancy data, not controlled studies; the underlying definition of "value-added time" is contested, and Nick Brown's own ASOS write-ups argue the metric is frequently gamed and misapplied. Use flow efficiency as a within-system trend and a conversation-opener, not as a pass/fail gate against an external number.

5. DORA's four keys do not transfer cleanly to a definition corpus. They were derived and validated for teams deploying software to production; a shop producing governance artifacts has no deployments, so any "DORA score" here is an analogy, not a measurement. What does transfer is the structural claim — throughput and stability move together in healthy systems — and the 2024 finding that this co-movement can break, which should caution against treating any single derived metric as diagnostic. The 2025 DORA "AI amplifies existing conditions" finding is survey-based and correlational; it is a useful frame, not proof.

6. Measuring this system risks the very dysfunction the sources warn about. Ridgway (1956), Campbell, and Strathern's Goodhart formulation all predict that publishing these factors as targets inside a system already inclined to generate conformance evidence will produce artifacts optimised against the factors. Mitigations: keep the factor set plural (SPACE's rule: at least three dimensions, never one number), keep at least one factor externally observed rather than self-reported, and re-derive the numbers independently rather than accepting the system's own tally. If these factors become an eighth check inside the corpus, they have failed.

7. The bureaucracy literature is largely about large organisations and has a strong prior against process. March/Schulz/Zhou studied a university over decades; Bozeman studied public agencies; Hamel & Zanini's BMI is a self-selected HBR-reader survey (n≈7,000, not a random sample) with an explicit anti-bureaucracy thesis. Applied to a 26-day-old, one-human, agent-staffed shop, these give mechanisms and vocabulary, not calibrated thresholds. Every numeric threshold in the factors above is either taken from a different domain (SQALE's 5%, DORA's bands) or proposed by me as a starting line; treat them as prompts for judgment, not as grades.

8. Two structural features of this system have no real literature behind them and should be flagged as genuinely uncharted. First, the constraint is not labour but one human's *attention*, and the producing capacity is effectively free and unbounded — no flow model in the sources was built for a system where supply of work-product is near-infinite and review capacity is fixed at one person. Second, the LLM instruction-following benchmarks (IFScale, ComplexBench, FollowBench) measure compliance with *synthetic, independently checkable* constraints; extrapolating from keyword-inclusion tasks to "can an agent apply a judgment-laden governance principle" is a real leap. The direction of the finding (more obligations, worse adherence, earlier obligations favoured) is robust; the specific numbers are not transferable.

9. On the 26-day question, the literature gives two defensible and opposed readings, and a reviewer should say so. The delivery frameworks (Agile, Shape Up, DORA) judge 26 days with no output harshly and unambiguously. The institutional and standards literature would say a foundation-laying phase producing no external output is normal and that judging it by delivery metrics is a category error. The tiebreaker available here is not a rule but an evidentiary one: was the foundation *tested* against anything external in that period? A foundation validated only by its own checks has no claim on the second reading — which is where the strongest finding in this analysis sits, and it does not depend on any particular threshold being right.
